World.title: Russia: Why is the Yabloko party barred from the elections?
World.content:
Russia's supreme court has banned the anti-war opposition party Yabloko from September's parliamentary elections. What does this mean for the election campaign, opponents of the war and for the political mood in Russia?

On Monday Russia's supreme court upheld a lawsuit against the anti-war opposition party Yabloko. Its candidates will now be barred from taking part in the parliamentary elections on September 18 to 20.

The case against Yabloko was brought by the pro-Kremlin party Rodina, which accused it of infringing copyright with its election campaign materials. Rodina also made the claim that Yabloko had engaged in extremist activities and had received illegal financing from abroad.

The verdict was pronounced by presiding judge Vyacheslav Kirillov. This was the same judge who, in April, banned the Russian human rights organization Memorial and designated it an extremist organization. Kirillov also previously dismissed legal complaints against the Russian prison service filed by the prominent opposition politician Alexei Navalny. Navalny spent many years in Russian prisons prior to his death in jail in 2024.

At least 500 people gathered in front of the Supreme Court to show their support for Yabloko. They distributed apples and sang songs. The name Yabloko – "apple" in English – derives from the initials of the party's three founders, Grigory Yavlinsky, Yury Boldyrev and Vladimir Lukin (YaBL). The apple is now well-known as a symbol of the party.

At the end of the nine-hour court session, security services threatened the people gathered outside the courthouse with arrest, also warning young men that they could be taken to an army enlistment office.

Several hundred people, most of them young, gathered outside the Supreme Court to await the outcome of the hearing Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance

"You are mistaken if you believe that, with a stroke of a pen, you can write off millions of people who want peace, freedom and a normal future for their country," Nikolai Rybakov, the leader of Yabloko, wrote on Telegram that evening.

He insisted that the party had not broken any Russian laws, and announced that he would appeal the judgement.

The Kremlin 'got scared'

Grigory Yavlinsky, one of the founders of Yabloko, said those in power were afraid of Yabloko's program, which calls for an election "for peace, freedom and a life without fear" – because, he said, "removing a party with a platform like this from the election, without any real grounds, is the political system exposing itself."

The lawsuit came at the same time as an appeal by Russian opposition and cultural leaders living abroad for people to support Yabloko.

They include the politician Yulia Navalnaya, Alexei Navalny's widow, as well as Lyubov Sobol, Ilya Yashin and Andrei Pivovarov. The writer Dmitry Bykov, human rights activist Oleg Orlov and other prominent people also voiced their support for Yabloko.

Navalnaya, who now leads the Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) her husband set up in 2011, responded to the verdict. The Kremlin was originally going to let Yabloko stand in the elections, she said, but those in power "got scared" and had the party blocked.

Navalnaya wrote on Telegram that the powers-that-be had observed a development they wanted to stop at any cost: People were starting to join forces. This, she wrote, was less about support for Yabloko than the possibility for millions of Russians to express how they really felt about Vladimir Putin and the war in Ukraine.

Andrei Pivovarov, a political activist who lives in exile in Germany and is a coordinator of the Russian Antiwar Committee , explained to DW that the opposition had not believed supporting Yabloko would bring about swift political change or an end to the war. The aim, he said, had been to make visible the extent of anti-war sentiment in Russia.

"There would have been a dozen parties on the ballot who are pro-war, and one that is pro-peace. The war wouldn't end even if Yabloko were to get representatives into the State Duma. But we would have seen that a lot of Russians oppose the war," said Pivovarov. This view, he added, would not simply disappear now Yabloko has been barred from standing.

What were the Kremlin's plans for Yabloko?

The political scientist Ivan Preobrazhensky speculated in an interview with DW that the banning of Yabloko could be a consequence of a power struggle between different interest groups in the Kremlin. He suggested that the security bloc allied with the federal security service, the FSB, may have wanted Yabloko to act as a counterweight to the New People party. This is regarded as a project of Sergey Kiriyenko, the first deputy chief of staff of the presidential administration.

Another version of events is that Kiriyenko himself may have tried to create the impression of political rivalry, and underestimated the potential of anti-war feeling in the country.

Yabloko party chairman Rybakov (right) with his lawyer, during the hearing Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance

Preobazhensky says the government underestimated the number of people in Russia who oppose the war and are ready to support a political force campaigning for an end to the war in Ukraine. Surveys, he says, indicate that there is substantial demand for such a political alternative. He also believes that the Kremlin initially intended to let Yabloko run in the election but changed its mind when it saw how much support the party was getting.

Another political scientist, Mikhail Vinogradov, thinks there was a different calculation behind the move. If Yabloko had scored very few votes in the election, the Kremlin could have painted a picture of a population solidly behind the war. A poor result would also have served to disillusion those who oppose it.

Barring Yabloko makes independent election monitoring more difficult. The party is now no longer allowed to send representatives to monitor polling stations. Roman Udot, a Russian specialist in electoral observation, explains that Yabloko has also enabled access for independent observers in the past.

Does the Kremlin have the situation under control?

The State Duma elections are taking place at a time of growing uncertainty in Russian society, says Margarita Zavadskaya from the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. She points to data from the Russian Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), which regularly records the population's prevailing view of the situation in the country: optimism or alarm?

At the end of July, 57% of those surveyed said that they were worried. This is the highest level since mobilization in the autumn of 2022. FOM surveys should be taken with a grain of salt, but Zavadskaya says an increase like this in high summer indicates that "something is not going according to plan."

She gives the increase in drone attacks, deaths, fires in warehouses and rumors of a fresh mobilization as the reasons, and comments that the summer of 2026 has been the most unsettling for the people in Russia since the beginning of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine. She also believes the number of people who support the war is going down rather than up.

The Russian leadership therefore has good reason to be nervous.

"For the Kremlin, the ideal scenario would be a boring election with low turnout and no noteworthy events," says Zavadskaya. "Right now, though, this seems unlikely, as the situation in the run-up to the election does not appear normal, nor does it give the impression that the government has the situation under control."

This article was originally written in Russian.

World.title: 25 years Ohrid Agreement: Is N. Macedonia's peace holding?
World.content:
A quarter of a century after the Ohrid Framework Agreement ended North Macedonia's 2001 conflict, analysts warn that peace between ethnic communities remains fragile.

The guns fell silent in 2001, but North Macedonia is still grappling with the legacy of its ethnic conflict.

Twenty-five years after the Ohrid Framework Agreement ended the fighting, ethnic Macedonians and Albanians live in peace, yet analysts say genuine reconciliation remains unattained.

The six-month conflict that erupted in February 2001 is often described as the final chapter of former Yugoslavia's violent breakup.

But unlike the wars in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, it was contained before it could spiral into a larger tragedy, thanks in large part to a political compromise brokered by NATO, the United States and leading EU countries.

Agreement enters a new phase

Тwenty-five years later, the political order that emerged from the Ohrid Framework Agreement is entering a new phase.

When the conservative Macedonian VMRO-DPMNE party returned to power two years ago, the Democratic Union for Integration (DUI), the main ethnic Albanian party, went into opposition.

This development ended two decades of governing influence for Ali Ahmeti, who transformed himself from leader of the ethnic Albanian National Liberation Army (NLA) during the 2001 conflict into one of the country's most influential political figures.

Ali Ahmeti, chairman of the ethnic Albanian DUI party, said recently that he sees 'serious signals about the direction in which the country is moving' Image: Petr Stojanovski/DW

Ahmeti, who swapped his guerrilla uniform for tailored black suits and white shirts after the Ohrid Agreement, now argues that ethnic relations have deteriorated over the past two years.

"Attacks on the official use of the Albanian language, the abolition of equitable and adequate representation, the weakening of mechanisms designed to prevent majoritarian rule and the promotion of a monoethnic concept of the state are serious signals about the direction in which the country is moving," he said in a statement marking August 2, North Macedonia's national holiday.

Balancing ethnic diversity and political stability

Home to a large ethnic Albanian minority, North Macedonia has spent much of the past quarter-century trying to balance its ethnic diversity within a stable political system.

According to the latest census, Albanians make up over a quarter of North Macedonia's population of 1.8 million.

For Bujar Osmani, a senior DUI official and former foreign minister, the key question is no longer how much of the Ohrid Agreement has been implemented, but whether its gains can be preserved.

"On the 25th anniversary of the Ohrid Agreement, the question is no longer only what we have implemented since 2001. The question is whether we will allow, within a few years, the dismantling of what has kept North Macedonia stable for two and a half decades," he told DW.

2001: A wound that has not fully healed

The legacy of the 2001 conflict runs deep.

The fighting claimed the lives of 72 soldiers and police officers, while the number of ethnic Albanian insurgents killed remains disputed, with estimates ranging from about 100 to several hundred. More than 170,000 people were displaced, including 74,000 within the country.

The Ohrid Framework Agreement that ended the conflict reshaped North Macedonia's political system, introducing power-sharing mechanisms designed to give minority communities a greater voice in decision-making.

Laws affecting sensitive issues such as language, education and national symbols require support not only from a parliamentary majority but also from representatives of minority groups.

Some 72 soldiers and police officers and between one and several hundred ethnic Albanian insurgents were killed in the conflict 25 years ago Image: Suki/epa/dpa/picture alliance

While largely in line with European standards on minority rights, the arrangement did not end disputes over equality and representation.

"The agreement achieved a large part of its historic mission, but its essence cannot be declared complete," Osmani said. "Ohrid is not an administrative checklist that can be fulfilled once and then archived. It is a system of balance that must be respected continuously."

Macedonian majority also voices grievances

At the heart of the debate are differing views on Ohrid's legacy.

While many ethnic Macedonians argue that affirmative representation policies have created unfair advantages for Albanians, Albanian politicians say the real concern is the gradual erosion of rights secured under the agreement.

"There is discrimination that frustrates many in the Macedonian community because Albanians are often given priority in recruitment to meet representation quotas in the public sector," said Stojance Angelov, a police general during the 2001 conflict.

Angelov said such practices put ethnic affiliation ahead of qualifications.

Osmani rejects that narrative, arguing that recent government policies have weakened protections for Albanians that were introduced after the conflict.

The six-month conflict began in February 2001 and is often referred to as the final chapter of the breakup of former Yugoslavia Image: epa/dpa/picture alliance

"At first, all of this was concealed behind political propaganda, technical explanations and claims that it was merely modernization of the system. Today, as that noise gradually fades, it is becoming much clearer what is actually being called into question," he said.

Defensive nationalism on the rise

Domestic and international observers warn that years of political crises and disputes over national identity have slowed reforms and reinforced ethnic divisions.

Harald Schenker of the German peacebuilding organization Pro Peace says the Ohrid Agreement transformed North Macedonia's institutions, but not necessarily relations between its communities.

"Ethnic distance is increasing, the education system remains segregated, and the two communities understand each other less and less," he told DW.

According to Schenker, the agreement created new institutions and rules of governance but failed to foster reconciliation or a shared vision for the future.

"Each side maintains its own interpretation of what happened in 2001," he said. "Twenty-five years on, there is a need for platforms where people can discuss these differences openly. Different perspectives exist, but people need to talk to one another."

Stalled EU integration

At the same time, years of stalled EU integration have fueled uncertainty about the country's direction. Although North Macedonia became an EU candidate country in 2005, negotiations have still not formally begun.

Former Foreign Minister Bujar Osmani said that the Ohrid Framework Agreement is 'not an administrative checklist that can be fulfilled once and then archived. It is a system of balance that must be respected continuously' Image: Anila Shuka/DW

After overcoming a decades-long dispute with Greece over its name, North Macedonia has faced new obstacles stemming from Bulgaria's demands relating to history, language and national identity.

The prolonged stalemate has not only frustrated reform efforts but has also deepened interethnic tensions, as the fading prospect of EU membership has removed one of the few unifying projects shared by both Macedonians and Albanians.

Against that backdrop, questions about North Macedonia's future remain closely tied to the legacy of the Ohrid Agreement. Next month, the country will mark 35 years since independence from the former Yugoslavia.

Osmani does not believe the country faces the risk of a new conflict but warns that ethnic tensions can build gradually.

"I do not believe citizens want a new problem," he said. "But ethnic tensions do not begin with conflict. They begin when one community gradually loses confidence that the system treats it as an equal."

Angelov shares that view.

"For me, the greatest achievement is that, whereas we once looked at each other through rifle sights, today I drink coffee with some of the veteran fighters of the Albanian NLA," he said.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: No oil, no salary: Iraqi state employees are feeling the crunch of the Hormuz blockade
World.content:
Because of the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, Iraq cannot export enough oil to fund the country's huge public sector. Protests have already started. Will the Iran war destabilize Iraq again?

They may be thousands of kilometers away but the Strait of Hormuz — or more specifically, its blockade — is making life increasingly difficult for many ordinary Iraqis.

For the last three months or so, Mahmoud Waleed's salary has been arriving later and later. The 38-year-old teacher is paid by the Iraqi Ministry of Education, but because Iraq cannot export enough oil through the Strait of Hormuz, the government is running out of cash.

As a result, thousands of Iraqis like Waleed are not being paid on time.

"The delay affects you a lot," the Mosul local told DW. "Like most people, we have financial obligations as well as basic living expenses. We're just more and more convinced that we need to reduce expenses and keep some money aside for emergencies — just until things return to normal. It makes you really anxious and fearful."

"The future looks more uncertain," adds Ahmed, a doctor from the same city who didn't want to give DW his full name for personal reasons. "This month, our salaries were delayed by more than 10 days. The Minister of Health explained the state doesn't have sufficient cash flow and that's why there was a delay. But we just don't know how long the next delay will be."

In early August, there were a number of small demonstrations about the delayed salaries. Staff from universities around the country protested as did employees at the Ministry of Electricity.

Before the war, Iraq was the fourth largest oil producer in the world, sitting behind sector heavyweights like Saudi Arabia and the US Image: Nabil Al-Jurani/AP Photo/picture alliance

Why doesn't Iraq have cash for salaries?

Almost all of Iraq's national budget, somewhere between 85% and 90%, comes from the export of its oil.

At the same time, Iraq has a huge and growing public sector, with about two-thirds of the around 30 million working-age Iraqis relying on the state for their livelihoods. That's why the majority of the state budget now goes towards salaries, pensions and social welfare; every month the Iraqi government needs somewhere between $6.5 billion and $8.2 billion for those payments.

But recently that money has become much harder to find.

Since Israel and the US bombed Iran in late February, Iran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz. Almost all of Iraq's oil — between 80% to 90% — was shipped out through there because unlike other countries in the region, Iraq doesn't have significant alternative routes.

As a result of the blockade, Iraqi oil exports decreased by around 83% in March, compared to the same period last year. By May, Iraq's seaborne crude exports were down 97%.

This means Iraq's national income has also been severely reduced. Government sources told various local media that Iraq's monthly income in May and June was somewhere between $2 billion and $2.3 billion, far less than is needed.

Iraq has also had to deal with much higher costs for shipping and insurance Image: Hussein Faleh/AFP

It's that kind of news that recently led to panicked rumors that state salaries would only be paid every 45 days, instead of each month.

Over the past few days, the Iraqi government put out several statements , firstly denying the 45-day rumor and then saying it still had $83 billion in reserves, plus gold holdings and non-oil income. This means salaries can be paid for the next 10 to 11 months, it said on Tuesday.

However that might not be enough. A report by UK advisory firm Oxford Economics this week noted that maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is unlikely to return to normal anytime soon.

"Until at least 2028, traffic levels are expected to fluctuate as tensions ebb and flow, while on average remaining well below pre-conflict norms," Ben May, director of global macro research said in a statement.

This is a serious crisis, one which "transcends the oil sector," Iraqi economist Ali Al-Rawi argued in an August report for Baghdad-based think tank the Al Bayan Center. "The entirety of the Iraqi economy is now hostage to… oil revenues."

In the first half of the year, new vehicle sales fell 28.6% in Iraq, reflecting the impact the cash crisis is having on the whole economy Image: Khalil Dawood/Xinhua/picture alliance

Iraq destabilized?

None of the state employees DW spoke to were planning to attend protests if their salaries were delayed again.

And right now, this situation is unlikely to destabilize Iraq, Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow at the British think tank Chatham House told DW.

"If salary delays continue, I would expect more protests, but initially they are likely to remain sectoral rather than develop into another nationwide movement like Tishreen," al-Shakeri said, referring to huge youth-led, anti-government protests between 2019 and 2021. "The government has learned from 2019 and now has a range of political, administrative and security mechanisms to contain protests before they broaden."

Things could get more dangerous later though if a combination of different problems arise, some of which have sparked larger protests in the past.

"If salary delays are combined with electricity shortages, inflation and deteriorating services over a sustained period, these separate protests could begin to connect," al-Shakeri predicts. "At that point, Iraq's recent stability would face a much more serious test."

What can Iraq do?

Iraq has tried to work around its Strait of Hormuz problem. A small proportion of Iraqi oil is exported via a Turkish pipeline. Oil has also been trucked out of Iraq, then loaded onto ships at Syrian ports. Last week, the Iraqi government announced it was reviving a long-shuttered Iraq-Lebanon pipeline.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi also said that when he visited Iran in late July, he asked Iranian officials for special dispensation allowing Iraqi oil to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The two countries have a good relationship.

Far more important, experts say, is that the new Iraqi government finally implement realistic reforms, measures that reduce corruption and encourage the private sector, moving the country away from oil dependency and offering locals jobs outside of the civil service.

But reforms also require funding — and the latest statistics indicate that this is not what is happening, researchers at economic consultancy Iraqi Horizons wrote this month.

In May, total government expenditure fell by around a quarter compared to last year. Of that, money for salaries, pensions and social security accounted for 99% of all operational spending. Which means there's very little cash left for anything else, the consultants pointed out.

"Fiscal crises have pushed Iraqi governments towards reform before," al-Shakeri from Chatham House suggested. "When oil revenues fall, governments become more willing to discuss combatting corruption, increasing non-oil revenues and supporting the private sector. But once oil money begins flowing again, the political incentives for reform weaken."

The current crisis could create an opening for reform in Iraq, al-Shakeri concluded. "But whether those openings survive once the immediate pressure eases is the real question."

World.title: Mozart tribute ends on sour note after mass figurine theft
World.content:
A playful tribute to Mozart has turned into a whodunit after 210 gold-colored figures disappeared from one of Austria's busiest tourist spots. The mass theft forced organizers to end the outdoor display early.

More than 200 gold-colored Mozart figures have vanished from a public art installation in Salzburg, forcing organizers to end part of the exhibition early.

The theft has disrupted a major public art project marking the 270th anniversary of composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's birth in his home city.

What do we know about the theft of the mini-Mozarts?

The Mozarteum Foundation said 210 of the 320 figures installed in the city's Mirabell Garden had disappeared. The theft forced organizers to end the garden display early.

Organizers had kept some replacements in reserve, but not enough to offset the scale of the theft.

The manufacturer is also on summer holiday, leaving no quick way to replace them.

Several dozen figures remain on display at the Mozarteum and Mozart's birthplace until the end of August.

The figures had been placed in the Mirabell Garden and at several Mozart-related sites around Austria's fourth-largest city.

German artist Ottmar Hörl said he thought the theft was cheeky, and organized Image: Matthias Schrader/AP Photo/picture alliance

The polymer figures show Mozart with his dog Pimperl, a nod to the composer's everyday life in Salzburg.

German conceptual artist Ottmar Hörl, who is behind the display, said he wanted to show Mozart not as a monument but "as a normal human being despite his genius."

Who might have taken the mini-Mozarts?

Hörl is known for installations made up of large numbers of identical figures depicting famous personalities.

"The worst thing for an artist is when his work dissolves," Hörl said.

Hörl said he did not believe tourists had simply walked off with the 50-centimeter (20-inch) figures.

"This is organized theft," he said, suggesting they were probably taken at night after the garden had closed. "I find it a bit cheeky."

Hörl had planned to sell the figures after the exhibition for around €90 each, putting the loss at roughly €20,000.

A previous Hörl display in Bayreuth suffered a similar fate when 100 figures of composer Richard Wagner disappeared.

"That's just the nature of public space," Hörl said. "When you work as an artist in a public space, you mustn't complain about what is happening there. It ranges from destruction to theft. That’s just how it is."

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

World.title: Unconstitutional? German intelligence to receive more powers
World.content:
German intelligence agencies have been calling for more powers in the fight against cyberattacks, terrorism and extremism. Now the government has given the go. Critics warn that red lines are being crossed.

The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (Bundesverfassungsschutz, BfV) and the Federal Intelligence Service (Bundesnachrichtendienst, BND) are secret services. Both operate covertly — the former domestically, the latter abroad. They have long complained that they have fewer powers than their counterparts in other countries.

To better defend Germany against internal and external threats, the cabinet approved a draft bill on Wednesday. Parliamentary approval is still pending; the MPs' summer recess ends in early September. However, it is considered a mere formality that the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, with the government majority of conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) and center-left Social Democrats (SPD), will give it the green light.

Germany's largest intelligence reform since World War II

A new era for the German intelligence services is then expected to begin in early 2027. Their scope of operations would extend far beyond their current powers. It would then be possible, for example, to counter a cyberattack by neutralizing enemy IT systems.

What is cyber warfare? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Should a state of tension or military defense arise, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) could carry out acts of sabotage abroad. In addition, the BND, like the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, would be given the ability to manipulate or delete data. Proponents and opponents alike agree that this reform would be the largest in German history since the end of World War II in 1945.

Intelligence services and police: Will they remain separate?

After World War II, as a lesson learned from the atrocities committed by the Secret State Police (Gestapo) during the Nazi era, separate areas of responsibility were established in West Germany. Since then, intelligence services have been primarily responsible for gathering information, while the police handle threat prevention and law enforcement. This so-called principle of separation is now in jeopardy.

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) speaks of "real intelligence agencies" and hopes that the planned reform will result in a more stable security architecture.

"Sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks and covert operations by foreign powers require new responses," Dobrindt said.

The agencies would be granted operational capabilities and active powers to effectively combat modern state terrorism and extremist violence.

AI and drones: Possibilities and Risks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Is the draft bill unconstitutional?

The BND and the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution are also set to be granted new powers in their traditional core mission of collecting and analyzing information. These include the analysis of large volumes of data using artificial intelligence (AI) and the cross-referencing of biometric data with the internet. Data retention periods are also set to be extended.

The Society for Civil Rights (GFF) considers large parts of the federal government's draft bill — which spans more than 700 pages — to be unconstitutional. With regard to the domestic intelligence service, the far-reaching access to private and public video surveillance in real time is seen as particularly problematic, GFF expert Kai Dittmann replied in response to a written inquiry from DW.

The donation-funded nonprofit GFF believes the same applies to biometric matching against publicly available images on the internet and the training of AI using data collected by intelligence agencies.

"There are no sufficient and clearly defined limits for such far-reaching intrusions, which above all affect countless innocent people," Dittmann criticizes.

The GFF argues the planned additional powers for the BND would violate constitutional rights: The foreign intelligence service would no longer be limited to gathering intelligence, but would also be tasked with warding off threats, operating domestically and carrying out active cyber operations.

"This blurs the constitutional boundaries between intelligence services, the police and the military," Dittmann says.

Germany's spy chief believes US cooperation will continue To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Will there still be parliamentary control?

The GFF also has serious concerns regarding the proposed reform of intelligence agency oversight, which is to be consolidated under the Independent Oversight Council. At the same time, there are plans to largely strip the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) of its authority to oversee intelligence activities. Dittmann's conclusion: "The agencies are gaining significantly more power, while oversight is likely to be weakened."

Clara Bünger, the domestic policy expert for the opposition socialist Left Party in the Bundestag, echoes this sentiment: "Because the intelligence agencies will no longer be required to inform those affected in many cases, effective legal protection is no longer guaranteed."

Bünger announced that the Left Party will oppose what they see as authoritarian restructuring of the state. "There must never again be a secret police in Germany," she said.

The Association of the Internet Industry (eco) has also expressed concerns: In light of the changing security landscape, intelligence agencies need modern technical capabilities, emphasizes board member Klaus Landefeld.

"But the line is crossed when the state develops an interest in keeping security gaps open so it can continue to have access. Vulnerabilities must be closed and must not become a tool for intelligence agency access," Landefeld added.

Meanwhile, Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the Parliamentary Oversight Committee for the Intelligence Services, has no such concerns.

"I believe it's time to trust our own government, including our own security agencies," the Christian Democrat said in a Table Media podcast.

Germany has the best-regulated intelligence services in the world, he said, and that should remain the case.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Eritrea: An emerging key player in the geopolitical gamble at the Horn
World.content:
Amid growing tensions and security risks at the Horn of Africa, Eritrea, with its strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea and a perceived lack of conflict, is emerging as important player in the region.

Across the Horn of Africa, geopolitical interests of various countries continue to cause tensions and conflict as part of the growing competition for political influence over the region.

In its own right, the small country of Eritrea appears to be gaining in importance within this context: The autocratic state run by long-standing ruler Isaias Afewerki controls strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea, especially with its ports of Assab and Massawa.

In July, a series of diplomatic consultations in Cairo involving regional powers like Egypt, Somalia, Eritrea, and a high-ranking US envoy highlighted Eritrea's growing role in helping to coordinate approaches to resolving serious security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea, and to facilitate trade.

Eritrea's unique location along this maritime route is notably becoming more and more strategic in light of international trade conflicts. The small nation's coastline near the Bab-al-Mandab Strait stretches for more than 1,000 kilometers (621.4 miles), bordering Sudan to the northwest and Djibouti to its southeast.

But Eritrea's main strategic importance relies on who is on the other side of the strait, which at its narrowest point measures fess than 30 kilometers.

A small country at a strategically important location

"Yemen lies on the other side of the Red Sea, which makes Eritrea's location particularly interesting, as Yemen is in a state of crisis and maritime security in the region is at risk," Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration (CRI) in London, told DW.

"The only safe route in this area runs through Eritrea, where there are currently no security concerns."

Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki has been ruling the country since its independence in 1993 as a strict one-party authoritarian regime Image: Khalil Senosi/AP Photo/picture alliance

The Houthi terrorist militia, propped up by Iran, have been attacking merchant ships in the Red Sea from the Yemeni coastline.

For the past ten years, Yemen has also been witnessing one of the world's worst humanitarian crises in its midst: Ongoing violence, economic collapse, droughts and floods have exacerbated the suffering in the country, according to a report published by the UN Refugee Agency last month.

Sayed meanwhile emphasizes that in Eritrea, the strong dictatorship entrenched for decades does not tolerate any type of dissent. In many international freedom indexes, the African nation often only comes second to North Korea.

Since the country was officially founded 32 years ago, there have been no elections in the one-party state under long-time ruler Afewerki.

A unique sense of stability — for now

But this is also exactly why there are no violent conflicts in the country. Compared to other players in the broader region like Ethiopia, Sudan, and Yemen, Eritrea appears to be an island of peace where it is easy to do business.

"For this reason, all countries — including regional powers such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt, which controls the Suez Canal — want to maintain stable relations with Eritrea," Sayed highlights.

At the same time, this could eventually prove to be the country's Achilles' heel: "The country is ruled by a single man, and there are no constitutional institutions. That makes the state very vulnerable should this strongman be removed from power," says Sayed.

There is no strong figure in the 80-year-old autocrat's inner circle seen as a clear successor. This has raised some concern that the security situation could collapse once the president might no longer be in power, according to Sayed.

This sailor from Yemen's internationally recognized government is in charge of controlling activity on the Red Sea Image: Khaled Ziad/AFP

Alternative to the Strait of Hormuz

Still, Eritrea continues to exert its influence as the Red Sea has now emerged as one of the the most important sea route in the world, especially for the Gulf states — Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, according to Sayed.

The war with Iran has further reinforced the nation's position, as this crisis has once again showed the central geopolitical importance of maritime chokepoints such as Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb.

One viable alternative, should the Strait of Hormuz remain repeatedly blocked, would be for these Gulf nations and their partners to find routes via Saudi ports located further up on the Red Sea.

While the Saudis have pipelines running from some of the interior regions of the country from where oil is extracted and produced to the port of Yanbu-Al-Bahr on the Red Sea, this alternative route could easily be compromised when it comes to security, potentially driving up oil prices even higher than what they currently are.

"For this reason, Eritrea today is of great strategic importance. This has been the case for centuries and will continue to be the case," Sayed emphasizes.

Why Ethiopia seeks control over Assab port To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ethiopia demands direct Red Sea access

Meanwhile, Eritrea's neighbors, particularly landlocked Ethiopia, are fighting hard to maintain access to the Red Sea as a trade route, Sayed adds, in particular for oil exports from the Horn of Africa to the rest of the world, especially to Europe and the Americas.

For decades, Djibouti has dominated regional trade logistics as Ethiopia's most important seaport partner, while Eritrea has been sidelined economically.

But Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has for years been demanding sovereign access to the sea — more than three decades after the country's split with Eritrea: when Eritrea gained its independence in 1993, Ethiopia lost its direct access, and has since been relying on its neighbors for all its sea trade.

However, maintaining a sense of neutrality and balance is proving to be a walk on a tightrope: Earlier 2026, the fragile relations with between Ethiopia and Eritrea's Asmara region had already threatened to escalate amid a dispute over Ethiopia's access to the maritime trade route.

Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The key context for Eritrea's recent strategic maneuvers in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea is the escalating tensions with Ethiopia," says Michael Woldemariam, a researcher at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland and the Atlantic Council.

"Asmara is seeking to forge partnerships that can serve as a counterweight to Addis Ababa. Its recent diplomatic outreach to Egypt, Somalia, the United Arab Emirates' armed forces, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopian opposition groups, and even the US should be viewed against this backdrop," he tells DW.

Meanwhile, a new trade corridor on the Red Sea is also taking shape: In May 2026, Eritrea and Egypt signed an agreement to establish direct freight connections between Egyptian and Eritrean ports on the Red Sea in order to expand independent trade and supply chains in the region.

A grave record of human rights violations

Still, there are no longterm guarantees with Eritrea, since the country's short history is almost entirely marked by violence, resulting in many people seeking a better life elsewhere.

"The first people fled Eritrea for Sudan in 1967 to escape [former Ethiopian ruler] Haile Selassie's imperial army. In the 1980s, people fled in large numbers from the Ethiopian military dictatorship. Since 2001, people have once again been fleeing in large numbers from human rights violations, military service, war, and a lack of prospects," says Magnus Treiber, a migration researcher specializing in the Horn of Africa at the Institute of Ethnology at the University of Munich.

"The causes of flight have hardly changed. However, since the European Union now offers virtually no opportunities to seek asylum, Eritreans are now fleeing all over the world."

Displacement is rife around the Horn of Africa, where various conflicts repeatedly force entire populations to seek safety elsewhere Image: GIULIA PARAVICINI/REUTERS

At least 700,000 people have left the country since its founding, which is about a fifth of its total population. The country's population growth meanwhile is under 2% — a low number compared to many countries in the region.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: El eclipse conquista el corazón de España
World.content:
A las ocho y media de la tarde, millones de personas miraron al mismo horizonte, asombrados ante un fenómeno astronómico irrepetible

Y el astro rey reveló por fin su corona. Lo hizo bajo un gigantesco manto de sombra que cruzó del norte al este de España a velocidad hipersónica, en apenas siete minutos, desde que entró por la costa cantábrica a las 20.26 hasta que salió por las Baleares a las 20.34 para fundirse con la noche en el mar Mediterráneo. El primer eclipse total que recorre el territorio peninsular desde 1905 cumplió con precisión astronómica los pronósticos; pero al mismo tiempo, sobrecogió a un país que lo esperaba y no recordaba nada semejante. A las ocho y media, el país entero se asomó asombrado hacia el mismo horizonte y más de una lágrima se derramó por las mejillas de quienes lo miraban, que luego se convirtió en una cascada, pero de mensajes que caían sin parar en los grupos de WhatsApp. “Yo también lo estoy viendo”, venían a decirse unos españoles a otros, en innumerables fotos y vídeos compartidos en redes.

Nadie que esté vivo había visto en estas tierras peninsulares esa corona solar, un sedoso velo blanco rodeando una estrella que emergió negra de golpe, casi una hora después de que la Luna nueva comenzase a eclipsarla. Una breve y extraña noche pasó durante un minuto escaso sobre al menos parte de 31 provincias españolas, que no volverán a ver algo así hasta el 17 de noviembre de 2180.

Valerio D'Orazio, de Lisboa (Portugal), utiliza una aplicación de su teléfono móvil para averiguar dónde se verá la fase de totalidad durante el eclipse solar total, en una fiesta para observar el eclipse celebrada en Buitrago del Lozoya (España), el 12 de agosto de 2026. Susana Vera (REUTERS) Una multitud de personas espera con gafas protectoras el comienzo del eclipse de Sol en Madrid este miércoles. SERGIO PEREZ (EFE) Ángela, David y su hijo Diego, de 7 años, posan para hacerse un selfi con gafas protectoras para eclipses durante la fiesta organizada para ver el eclipse solar en Buitrago del Lozoya, España, el 12 de agosto de 2026. Susana Vera (REUTERS) Un hombre prueba unas gafas especiales para observar el eclipse, este miércoles en una playa de Valencia. Alberto Saiz (AP Photo/Alberto Saiz) La Luna comienza a ocultar el Sol en Arija (Burgos). Borja Suarez (REUTERS) Un grupo de personas siguiendo el eclipse en San Sebastián de los Reyes. ÁLVARO GARCÍA Cientos de personas esperan el inicio del eclipse solar en la playa de Riazor en Coruña, este miércoles. Lavandeira (EFE) Un grupo de personas sigue el eclipse desde San Sebastián de los Reyes, este miércoles. ÁLVARO GARCÍA Un paracaidista baja durante el eclipse, en la playa Gurugú en Castellón. Carme RIPOLLE Carme Ripolles El eclipse visto desde San Sebastián de los Reyes. Alvaro Garcia Detalle del eclipse, visto desde Arija. Borja Suarez (REUTERS) Imagen compuesta formada por siete fotografías tomadas con una única cámara fija que muestra las distintas fases de un eclipse solar, antes y durante la totalidad, observado desde Arija (España), el 12 de agosto de 2026. Borja Suarez (REUTERS) Una mujer sorprendida mientras contempla el eclipse en Mora la Nova, provincia de Tarragona. GIANLUCA BATTISTA Eclipse Solar desde el Castillo de Montjuic de Barcelona. Massimiliano Minocri Personas congregadas en Benavente, (Zamora), presencian el eclipse en su fase de totalidad. Emilio Fraile Eclipse de Sol junto a un toro de Osborne este miércoles en la localidad de Pradorrey (León). Borja Sanchez-Trillo (EFE) Jazz de Ría Rocío Cibes 12/08/26 ROCÍO CIBES Eclipse solar desde peña izquierda en el Puerto de Montenegro , Soria Victor Sainz Una mujer observa el Sol desde el campo de fútbol de la calle Teide, en San Sebastián de los Reyes. Álvaro García Ambiente previo al eclipse, cerca de un acantilado en Cedeira. ROCÍO CIBES Una mujer fotografía este martes el atardecer y el Cañón del Sil desde el Mirador de Matacás, en Castro Caldelas (Ourense), un día antes del eclipse solar. Brais Lorenzo (EFE) El francés Leyssalle Anthony, de 39 años, prepara un telescopio para observar el eclipse solar total desde la playa de Arija (Burgos), este miércoles. Borja Suarez (REUTERS)

La meteorología también cumplió esta vez con su parte en buena parte de la franja de totalidad. Al menos 15 millones de personas ubicadas bajo esa sombra de unos 300 kilómetros de ancho, prácticamente libre de nubes para la ocasión, tuvieron la oportunidad de mirar directamente el espectáculo natural de un eclipse total perfecto, algo que no puede verse desde ningún otro punto del sistema solar. Solo en la Tierra; y, este 12 de agosto, solo en parte de Islandia y de España, los únicos territorios habitados por los que cruzó la banda de totalidad de este eclipse. En declaraciones a los medios desde el Observatorio de Yebes (Guadalajara), punto oficial de seguimiento del eclipse, el presidente de la Comisión Interministerial para el Trío de Eclipses y secretario de Estado de Ciencia, Innovación y Universidades, Juan Cruz Cigudosa, aseguró que esta cita convertiría a España en “el Mundial de la Astronomía”. “Hoy es la final. España está jugando la final. Está liderando la final”, subrayó. Y desde luego España ganó esa final, para desgracia de los islandeses, que no pudieron ver nada: nubarrones y lluvias opacaron el paso del eclipse por el extremo occidental de la isla, donde Björk había organizado una “rave” solar.

La España vaciada, donde las condiciones eran idóneas para observar el fenómeno, esperaba con la mayor expectación este eclipse. Provincias casi siempre alejadas de la atención, como Soria, Palencia, Teruel o León, concentraron las miradas de todo el mundo y fueron anfitrionas de una celebración única en medio de un verano plagado de romerías. Los festivales masivos de música cedieron el protagonismo a fiestas populares en honor a la alineación perfecta del Sol y la Luna, planeadas con mimo en localidades como Castrillo de la Reina (Burgos), donde la charanga comenzó a recorrer sus estrechas calles a las seis de la tarde, anunciando la doble noche que se avecinaba. Este pueblo, que en invierno solo tiene 121 habitantes, fue el campamento base para más de mil personas llegadas de toda España, que guardaron con celo el secreto de esta ubicación privilegiada ante la posibilidad de una afluencia masiva. A Castrillo de la Reina llegó también una delegación de periodistas del periódico estadounidense The New York Times, que pondría en el centro de atención mundial a esta pequeña localidad de la Sierra de la Demanda. Periodistas internacionales y un festival con aficionados llegados de toda España para ajetrear un pequeño pueblo, perfecta ilustración de lo que supuso este fenómeno astronómico en buena parte de los pequeños municipios que se vieron regados con el premio de la lotería cósmica. “Va a ser como un atardecer sin atardecer”, comentan emocionadas unas adolescentes de Castrillo, ataviadas con las gafas eclipseras en la frente como si fueran gafas de sol fashion.

00:51 Reacciones al eclipse solar total en España 12.08.2026 El eclipse visto desde Riaño (Castilla y León). Foto: Néstor Rodan | Vídeo: EPV

La idea de verse desbordados con concentraciones multitudinarias, en medio de un verano que está surfeando una ola de calor tras otra, era la gran preocupación en esa España que enseñaba con orgullo observatorios astronómicos privilegiados como el de Javalambre (Teruel) o que sentía reconocida la bella oscuridad de sus cielos en provincias como Guadalajara, donde las noches de verano que muestran miles de estrellas invisibles en las ciudades, y revelan la Vía Láctea, han sido un auténtico semillero de vocaciones para docenas de astrónomos de primera fila internacional. Esa España que tiende un puente científico con Marruecos —en tiempos tan complicados con el vecino del sur— para ensayar en la ciudad de Palencia un experimento científico que se completará el 2 de agosto de 2027, cuando otro eclipse total cruce el extremo sur de la Península y el norte de África.

Si lo normal es que pasen casi 400 años para que un eclipse total vuelva a pasar por el mismo lugar, las regiones que han vivido este miércoles el día de las dos noches pueden considerarse especialmente afortunadas. Otro eclipse con un recorrido muy similar pasó por la mayoría de ellas en 1905, dejando huella en la memoria colectiva. En Castrillo de la Reina, los más viejos del lugar recuerdan cómo sus mayores les hablaron de aquella vez que la gran sombra de la Luna les cogió por sorpresa, hace 121 años y también a mediados del siglo XIX. Aunque el país entero llevase meses hablando del fenómeno astronómico, cuyo paso la ciencia había predicho al segundo, cuando de verdad llegó dejó una mezcla de júbilo y estupor que nos hizo empatizar con nuestros antepasados que vivían con miedo esa súbita oscuridad, que siempre llegaba por sorpresa.

La eclipsemanía pasó por España por primera vez desde que toda la población tiene acceso libre a la información sobre los detalles de la ocultación total del Sol —y a los medios de protección adecuados para observar el fenómeno sin riesgos para la vista—, resucitó preocupaciones que conectan con algunos de esos miedos ancestrales. Colegios de oftalmólogos y departamentos ministeriales recomendaron a la población que observase el eclipse total con las gafas de protección puestas todo el tiempo, ante el temor a graves lesiones oculares por su uso incorrecto. Mientras tanto, pequeños pueblos como Frómista (Palencia) prefirieron organizar observaciones públicas con maestros de ceremonias como el astrofotógrafo Ángel de Francisco, que dio precisas indicaciones a sus vecinos sobre cuándo tenían que quitarse las gafas para poder observar, sin riesgos, lo que siempre está ahí pero nunca habíamos podido ver: la corona solar.

Un reto para el país

Justo cuando la Luna comenzaba a morder la luz del Sol, el ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, informaba en Yebes de que el comienzo del operativo —que había anunciado el despliegue de casi 35.000 efectivos, entre policías y guardias civiles— se había desarrollado sin demasiados incidentes. A primera hora de la tarde, algunos atascos a la salida de Madrid y Barcelona, que no se habían llevado el premio gordo del eclipse total, mostraban las ganas de la ciudadanía de llegar a un evento único. Atascos que se repitieron entrada la noche, de regreso. Y también en la costa asturiana, castigada por las nubes.

El Gobierno instaló su cuartel general en el Observatorio Astronómico de Yebes, levantado en 1975 en este pueblo de Guadalajara de más de 5.600 habitantes por sus casi 1.000 metros de altitud, pero a pesar de los rumores, desmentidos desde La Moncloa, no apareció por allí Pedro Sánchez, que solo disfrutó de un eclipse parcial en la residencia de La Mareta, en la isla canaria de Lanzarote. Aunque la totalidad del 100% oculto solo ensombreció al 40% del territorio español, todo el país, hasta el archipiélago canario, disfrutó de su trocito de eclipse.

01:43 Seis lugares distintos que han visto el eclipse Varias personas observan el eclipse en Arcos de Salinas (Teruel), este miércoles. Foto: Christian Hartmann (REUTERS) | Vídeo: EPV

El Gobierno preveía entre 400.000 y 1,5 millones de desplazamientos adicionales para acudir a zonas donde el fenómeno se observara en su totalidad, por lo que se había desplegado un dispositivo especial de vigilancia de la Dirección General de Tráfico. También se temía una caída de las comunicaciones por saturación y, sobre todo, había temor por el riesgo de incendios, como señaló la ministra para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico, Sara Aagesen: “Prohibido encender fuego, no aparcar sobre vegetación seca, mantener los accesos libres para emergencias y consultar diariamente el nivel de peligro de incendios. El día del eclipse solar total es un día para disfrutar, pero también una llamada a la prudencia y a la precaución”.

El cálculo de los beneficios para las provincias agraciadas por la lotería astronómica estimaba medio millón de turistas extra gracias al astroturismo y entre 350 y 400 millones de euros de valor añadido. Pero la ciencia tomó la palabra para reivindicarse en tiempos oscuros, y no por la sombra del eclipse. El astronauta, exministro de Ciencia y presidente de Hispasat, Pedro Duque, expresó su deseo de que el eclipse “atraiga a la gente hacia el conocimiento” y de que “quede en la conciencia” de los españoles. En declaraciones a los medios en el Observatorio del Ebro, en Roquetes (Tarragona), insistió en luchar contra la desinformación con el poder de la ciencia: “Hay gente que hace más caso a un audio de WhatsApp que te viene de la vecina del quinto que a las cosas que realmente funcionan, como la ciencia”.

En ese mismo sentido, su sucesora, Diana Morant, defendió en RNE que “es imposible una conversación entre ciencia y un charlatán”. “La humanidad siempre ha mirado al cielo para explicar las cosas y cuando no existía la ciencia se pensaba que eran los dioses los que castigaban”, dijo la ministra. “Se buscaban explicaciones y ahora las explicaciones las tenemos en la ciencia y no hay una ciencia que explique el cambio climático y una ciencia que diga que no hay cambio climático”, insistió. Más allá de la confrontación política, una cita científica, un eclipse total histórico, llenó de asombro a media España, hipnotizada por la belleza de la imagen que grabó en sus retinas.

World.title: Arranca el mayor escaparate de las estrellas del mundo
World.content:
23 de los 52 jugadores convocados para la final del Mundial y 18 campeones juegan en LALIGA. Ninguna de las grandes ligas europeas supera el dato. La competición arranca este viernes con nuevas caras y viejos conocidos que elevan el nivel del torneo

No hay que esperar cuatro años para volver a ver a las mejores estrellas del fútbol mundial: en LALIGA, juegan cada fin de semana. La temporada 2026/2027 arranca este fin de semana con un dato que refleja el talento del fútbol profesional español: 23 de los 52 jugadores convocados por España y Argentina para la final del Mundial juegan en la máxima competición del fútbol español, así como 18 campeones que contribuyeron a que en la camiseta de la selección española figuren ahora las dos estrellas.

totales en 3.318 Goles

totales en 601 Asistencias

totales en 377 Edad media 26,42 años El XI de los Campeones del mundo con más partidos en LALIGA Unai Simón 237 Eric García 145 Aymeric Laporte 186 Marcos Llorente 270 Pedri 201 Marc Cucurella 143 Ferran Torres 211 Álex Baena 173 Mikel Oyarzábal 349 Nico Williams 157 Borja Iglesias 291 *Se incluyen datos de LALIGA EA SPORTS y LALIGA HYPERMOTION.

El logro del trofeo más prestigioso del fútbol ha propiciado que la primera jornada se haya dividido para esperar la vuelta de las merecidas vacaciones de los campeones. Entre el sábado 15 y el miércoles 19 de agosto se disputarán siete partidos de LALIGA EA SPORTS. Los tres restantes, aplazados para que los equipos puedan contar con todos sus futbolistas, se disputarán a finales de mes: el Valencia-Real Betis, el día 25; el Real Madrid-Real Sociedad, el 26 y cerrará la jornada el 27 el FC Barcelona-Athletic Club, dos de los equipos que más jugadores aportaron al combinado español con 11 estrellas. Por su parte, el pistoletazo de salida a LALIGA HYPERMOTION será el viernes 14 con el duelo que enfrenta al filial de la Real Sociedad contra el CD Castellón, una de las revelaciones de la pasada campaña que se quedó a las puertas del ascenso.

Como cada temporada, los equipos ultiman sus plantillas. Llegan nuevas caras y viejos conocidos que elevan el nivel de LALIGA EA SPORTS. Nombres como el de Sergio Canales, que regresa al R. Racing Club tras una estancia en México; Anthony Gordon, estrella de la selección inglesa que llega al FC Barcelona o el de José Mourinho, en su vuelta al banquillo del Real Madrid.

Nuevas caras y viejos conocidos en LALIGA EA SPORTS José Mourinho REAL MADRID El portugués José Mourinho releva esta temporada a uno de sus alumnos más aventajados, Álvaro Arbeloa, en el banquillo madridista. En su anterior etapa (2010-2013) dirigió al conjunto blanco en 114 partidos –84 victorias– en LALIGA EA SPORTS y logró el título liguero en la campaña 2011/12. Foto: Diario AS Diomande REAL MADRID El fichaje del extremo costamarfileño, titular en el pasado Mundial con su selección, llega para reforzar el ataque del Real Madrid. Ya disputó diez partidos con la camiseta del CD Leganés (dos goles y una asistencia) en la temporada 2024/25. En la imagen, montaje elaborado por el Real Madrid para anunciar su fichaje. Foto: Real Madrid Canales R. Racing Club El canterano racinguista debutó en LALIGA EA SPORTS el 10 de octubre de 2008 con el equipo santanderino. Pasó por el Real Madrid, el Valencia CF y la Real Sociedad; brilló en el Real Betis (164 partidos ligueros, 30 goles y 25 asistencias) y ahora vuelve a su tierra tras tres años en la liga mexicana. Foto: Diario AS Grimaldo Atlético de Madrid A sus 30 años, el campeón del mundo (en la imagen, con el trofeo) tiene un nuevo reto en su carrera: debutar en LALIGA EA SPORTS. Mandi, internacional con Argelia en 114 ocasiones y capitán, jugó 206 partidos en la máxima categoría del fútbol profesional español entre 2016 y 2024, primero en el Real Betis y luego en el Villarreal CF. En la imagen, el central, en una disputa con Lionel Messi durante el Mundial. Ahora, llega a LALIGA EA SPORTS pese al interés de equipos de la Premier League y la Serie A italiana. En la imagen, durante uno de los entrenamientos de pretemporada. En la imagen, el extremo (a la izquierda), durante la preparación veraniega. En la categoría de plata anotó 14 goles, repartió 8 asistencias en 42 partidos. Ahora, el fichaje del RCD Espanyol de Barcelona tiene la oportunidad de hacerse un hueco en la élite. Foto: Diario AS Chupe, Larrubia y Joaquín Málaga CF El tridente ofensivo del Málaga CF la pasada temporada: entre los sumaron 43 goles y 17 asistencias para devolver al equipo donde se formaron a la élite nueve años después. La jornada empieza en el bar

Los aficionados que quieran vivir el fútbol en un ambiente diferente también pueden hacerlo en los miles de bares que cuentan con los paquetes oficiales de retransmisión. Con un doble valor añadido: los futboleros que decidan acudir a su establecimiento de confianza contribuyen al crecimiento y a la dinamización del sector HORECA y refuerzan, con su visita, la cultura de la previa y el pospartido, lo que demuestra que el fútbol también puede ser una experiencia social que va mucho más allá de los 90 minutos.
