World.title: Lasha Bugadze becomes first modern Georgian writer whose book was barred from being sent to prison
World.content:
Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

The administration of Rustavi Prison refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel, The Observer, to be delivered to the prison. The book was intended for Nana Sander, who was convicted over her participation in a protest on 4 October 2025.

Notably, the penitentiary code contains no provision explicitly banning fiction from being brought into prisons.

The book’s synopsis describes a fictional political reality involving the long rule of a “despot”, the “division of the country into zones” and a “cult of the leader”. It also mentions the scheduling of elections and a decision by the country’s population on whether they should take place.

According to Bugadze, a prison official refused to allow the book in, saying the novel contained “political content”.

The writer says it is unclear to him who determined that the book contained political content and what criteria they used. He suspects the decision may have been prompted by words and phrases in the novel, such as “despot” and “cult of the leader”.

“The employee told me directly that the book could not be delivered because it was political in nature. I don’t think he sat down and read the book. I doubt he even read the synopsis,” Bugadze said.

In his view, someone appears to have judged the work to be political without giving any clear reason.

“Who put this label on the text? [Who decided] whether it was political or not? What does that even mean? And, excuse me, even if the content is political, why should a citizen – whether a prisoner or anyone else – not have the right to read such a book?” the writer said.

Bugadze sees the incident as a potential precedent for censoring literary works:

“It can be described as the first significant example of literary censorship in modern Georgian history. This is an extremely dangerous precedent, and under no circumstances should it be considered normal. The situation requires a response. No one has the right to stop someone from reading.”

The head of the human rights organisation Sapari, Baia Pataraia, announced that legal proceedings would begin over the incident:

“We are taking legal steps. <…> First, we will demand a written and reasoned refusal.”

The organisation PEN Georgia also responded to the case. It described the incident as an alarming precedent for censorship of a literary work, linked not only to the novel’s content but also to the author’s political and civic stance. The organisation stressed that censoring fiction and restricting freedom of expression are unacceptable in a democratic society.

Lasha Bugadze’s The Observer

Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Kobakhidze: Georgia does not publicly declare Russia an enemy because this would require follow-up steps
World.content:
Georgian prime minister on Russia

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that the Georgian government does not publicly call Russia an “enemy” because such a political statement would require corresponding action.

A journalist asked Kobakhidze whether the Georgian government considers Russia an enemy. The prime minister replied:

“Your questions are shameful, you look ridiculous. Let me explain in simple terms why this question is shameful: you want to get a sensational headline, even in the Russian media, saying that I have declared the Russian Federation an enemy. This is a specific political statement that would have to be followed by specific steps – roughly the same, or exactly the same, as those your party” (referring to the United National Movement – JAMnews) “took in 2008 and before.”

The journalist asked whether this was precisely why the government was reluctant to openly call Russia an enemy.

“Of course. What, should I repeat it again?!” Kobakhidze replied.

Kobakhidze also addressed Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and reiterated that the Russian Federation occupies 20% of Georgia’s territory.

“Of course, the Russian Federation is the only state and party that has occupied Georgian territories. This is an absolutely clear fact. Numerous statements have been made about this, and there is no doubt about it,” Kobakhidze stressed.

He said Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory was a “crime against the Georgian state and the Georgian people”:

“This is an egregious crime: first the occupation, and then the so-called recognition.”

Georgian prime minister on Russia

World.title: Bizarre new astronomical object dubbed a 'black hole star'
World.content:
Is it a star or a black hole? A recently discovered astronomical object appears to be a bizarre mix of both.

About the size of the solar system and shrouded in a cloud of gas, the object produces 100 billion times the energy of any known star.

The object, spotted with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), is so strange astronomers have dubbed it a "black hole star."

And while it is the first of its kind to be described, the researchers who spotted it can already tell it is far from the last.

The discovery, published today in Nature, could help reveal the identity of mysterious "little red dots" detected in images of the early cosmos taken by the JWST.

Lead researcher Rohan Naidu, an astronomer at the University of Hawaii, said the black hole stars had "remarkable physics".

"We are excited to be studying a new kind of astrophysical object," Dr Naidu said.

"There's so much to do."

Strange little red dots may be 'black hole stars'

When JWST started beaming imagery back to Earth, astronomers found something they were not expecting in the data: specks they have named "little red dots", or LRDs.

These dots hail from the very early universe: between roughly 650 million and 1.6 billion years after the big bang.

Little red dots, circled here in blue, showed in the James Webb Space Telescope's imagery. (Supplied: NASA, UNCOVER team and Karl Glazebrook)

This research used JWST to investigate one of these little red dots, MoM-BH*-1, more closely.

Light from this dot comes from 660 million years after the big bang, and has travelled across space for more than 13 billion years.

They found that light from the dot had not come from stars or the dust that permeated interstellar space.

Instead, it was likely coming from very dense hydrogen and helium gas.

The researchers ran a series of simulations to come up with an object that could explain the signals they were seeing from JWST.

"It took me a few months of continuously searching for a model that was a good match to the data," Dr Naidu said.

That model is a huge, young black hole, surrounded not by dust or stars like older black holes are, but by pristine gas.

The researchers suggest that bluer light from the black hole is absorbed by the gas, causing the red dot appearance. (ABC Science)

The researchers have called it a black hole star, because it resembles a massive star, but powered by a black hole at its centre.

Nicholas Seymour, an astronomer at Curtin University who was not involved with the study, said the object had roughly a million times the mass of Earth's Sun.

"That sounds enormous, but compared with the billion-solar-mass monsters we see in the early universe, it is relatively small," Dr Seymour said.

The black hole itself would only be about eight times the size of the Sun, but the gas around it would be about the size of the solar system.

"Imagine an object with the mass of a million Suns hidden inside a turbulent cloud stretching across our solar system," Dr Seymour said.

MoM-BH*-1 is one of the "little red dots" that have shown up unexpectedly in JWST imagery. (Supplied: Nature)

Christian Wolf, an astronomer at the Australian National University who also was not involved with the study, called it "the most exciting black hole to be reported in years of black hole research".

"It shows that the state these black holes are in is unlike anything we have seen traditionally," Professor Wolf said.

"This is the first 'supermassive black hole teenager' humanity has seen.

"The good thing is, it points us to the environmental conditions in which these early black holes developed their identity and physical nature."

Dr Naidu said that he and other researchers had since studied 100 other little red dots.

"We found that indeed, a gas-enshrouded heart, remarkably similar to MoM-BH*-1, lies at the centre of every little red dot," he said.

Which came first, black hole or star?

Professor Wolf said that the finding added evidence to a changing theory about the universe's formation.

"For a long time most researchers took it for granted that black holes were first seeded by the collapse of massive short-lived stars in the early universe, and then grew from there," he said.

While this does happen in today's universe, the discovery of black hole stars suggests that supermassive black holes can form without surrounding galaxies.

"Here we see a naked black hole evolving into something big, and there is no sign of a galaxy with stars around it," Professor Wolf said.

The new object appears to be a black hole in a massive field of gas that radiates like a star. (Supplied: Rohan Naidu/University of Hawai'i)

This adds to the theory that, in the early universe, giant black holes were formed by something other than a collapsing star.

"The black holes seem to come first and then be seeds for galaxy formation around them," Professor Wolf said.

"Again, a new, more powerful telescope shows us that our imagination is curiously limited until we turn it on, get a better view and see more magic than we have deemed plausible."

While JWST discovered these objects, other telescopes like radio telescopes may help to study them further with new streams of data.

Dr Seymour has been using the Murchison Widefield Array and the Australian SKA Pathfinder telescopes in Western Australia to look for black holes from the early universe.

"Our work suggests that we may be able to find many more of these objects, potentially catching black holes at even earlier stages of their growth," he said.

"If so, we could be getting closer to solving one of astronomy's biggest puzzles: how did the first supermassive black holes grow so big, so quickly?"

World.title: 'Gang mentality': Former jihadist tells inquiry how he left extremism
World.content:
A former Salafi jihadist-turned undercover operative has told the antisemitism royal commission how he became radicalised after an encounter with the Taliban.

After radicalising as a young man, Mubinoddin Shaikh became disillusioned with extremism following the 9/11 terror attacks.

He said in his work combating extremism in the decades since, he observed that antisemitism appeared to be the "connective tissue" across different ideologies.

On Thursday, Mr Shaikh appeared at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, which has been examining pathways to violent extremism and subsequent disengagement with harmful ideologies.

Mr Shaikh grew up in a conservative Muslim household in Toronto, Canada, and said he travelled to Pakistan in mid-1995 on an immersive religious tour with the Tablighi Jamaat Islamic movement.

Prior to this, he said he had been shamed by his uncle after being caught "red handed" throwing a house party while his parents were out of town; an incident which Mr Shaikh described as pivotal to setting him on the path to religious extremism.

Mr Shaikh says he "became enamoured" with the Taliban in his youth. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

While visiting mosques and interacting with Pakistani locals, Mr Shaikh had a chance encounter with members of the Taliban carrying weapons.

"One of them responded, 'If you want to succeed in this life and the next, you do it with this'. And then he picked up the AK-47," he told the commission.

He said he "became enamoured" with the men and their beliefs at a time when he was seeking a sense of belonging.

"I wanted to be like them, I wanted to join them," he said.

"I thought I had found the group that I should have been with."

'Gang mentality'

Upon his return to Canada, Mr Shaikh left the Tablighi Jamaat and joined an extremist Salafist group.

The group discussed geopolitical events and wars, and talked about going to fight in Chechnya, where Russia had invaded, but were dissuaded from doing so.

"Going overseas and fighting the great jihad was that umbrella desire … that we all had," he said.

Mr Shaikh says he began distancing himself after getting married. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

"It became like a gang mentality in many ways when we would walk around with our brothers … we really felt empowered.

" We knew that we were intimidating people. "

Mr Shaikh met regularly with the group between 1995 and 1998, but started to disengage with their activities after he married and started to plan for a family of his own.

Path to deradicalisation

He said the trigger point for his deradicalisation came after the 9/11 attacks in New York City, saying he struggled to reconcile the acts of mass violence with Islam.

"While we were talking about these foreign wars that were happening in the name of Islam and how that was all legitimate, now that fight got brought to the home front," he said.

" Especially seeing planes fly into buildings … I could not understand how this fit into the Islamic war tradition. "

Meanwhile, he said others in his Salafist group were "jubilant" over the attacks, prompting him to sever ties and begin the journey to deradicalisation.

In subsequent years, he pursued Arabic and Islamic studies and studies around Sufi spirituality in Syria.

He was later recruited to be an undercover operative with the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.

He was also involved in counter-ISIS activities for the US military.

Since deradicalising, Mr Shaikh has worked for a counter-terrorism agency and the US military. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

Mr Shaikh now works with Peace for Parents, a not-for-profit that supports families and other groups affected by extremism.

He works one-on-one with young people referred to the program by parents, guardians or schools concerned about their behaviour or beliefs.

He said the group had recently established a specific intervention strategy for antisemitism-related cases.

"Seventy per cent of our cases show some kind of antisemitic influence," he said.

"Antisemitism appears to be the connective tissue across extremist ideologies."

World.title: 'All women feel it': Four killed in alleged violence in less than two months in Qld
World.content:
Four women have been killed in alleged violent incidents in Queensland in less than two months, a statistic that advocates say should unite the community in grief.

Queensland Domestic and Family Violence Prevention Minister Amanda Camm said the killings were "abhorrent".

"All women feel it when a woman is murdered, as I'm sure many men in our community do," she said.

"It will take society and a whole-of-community approach, frankly, to get back to the basics around respect for each other."

Counting Dead Women Australia, a register that tracks homicides of women, says 30 women have died this year to date.

A 27-year-old woman was found dead in Logan, south of Brisbane, in the early hours of Wednesday.

Her former partner, 37-year-old Ronald Arthur Claren Cora, has been charged with murder as a domestic violence offence.

The 27-year-old woman was found dead at a home in Slacks Creek in the early hours of Wednesday. (ABC News: Jordan Bissel)

Police said the man and woman were the only people in the house.

Last week, the body of Julia Brunsdon was found in the outback town of Charleville, about 750 kilometres west of Brisbane, alongside her partner Michael Waltke's, in a suspected murder-suicide.

Police confirmed the 23-year-old was pregnant.

Police confirmed the man and woman found dead in a suspected murder-suicide were in a relationship. (ABC News: Will Murray)

Weeks earlier, the body of Jana Armstrong was found, ending a four-day search for the Toowoomba mother, who leaves behind a baby boy.

The body of Jana Armstrong, 30, was found last month after a four-day search. (Supplied: Faith Isaacs)

Her former partner Dharminder Singh has been charged with one count of murder, as a domestic violence offence.

On June 28, 23-year-old Mallorie Roberts was declared dead on the Gold Coast.

Mallorie Roberts has been remembered as a kind, loving and gentle soul. (Supplied: Felicity Jane)

She was allegedly shot, with police recovering a homemade firearm from the home that they believe was used in the shooting.

Ethan Midgely, believed to be her partner, has been charged with murder as a domestic violence offence and unlawful possession of a weapon used to commit an indictable offence.

Today Ms Camm announced an additional $3.3 million in state government funding to improve intake and assessment processes for key frontline domestic violence prevention services.

Qld government denies blocking domestic violence report The report was particularly critical of police responses to domestic and family violence incidents.

She said it was important to "improve system performance", find new ways to respond, and ensure that when a call or referral is received, the best system is in place to intake the person seeking help.

Chief executive of the Centre Against Domestic Abuse, Holly Brennan, who stood alongside Ms Camm at today's announcement, said her organisation had seen an uptick in those reaching out for help.

"In the last year, we've supported over 1,000 additional people as an example of this," she said.

"Victim survivors need to have a service system that can be responsive at their time of need."

Shadow treasurer, Shannon Fentiman said the alleged murders were "devastating, heartbreaking, harrowing and preventable".

"I say to premier David Crisafulli and Minister Amanda Camm, where is the urgency? Where is the emergency response? Where is the funding for DV prevention?"

Action on improving women's safety questioned

Ms Camm and the Queensland government have been under fire for cuts to domestic violence prevention funding, and the reallocation of millions of dollars from the portfolio to areas where it could not be promised it would wholly benefit victims of domestic violence.

Today Ms Camm was questioned about the progress of 277 recommendations made to the state government by the Women's Safety and Justice Taskforce across two reports handed down in 2021 and 2022.

Amanda Camm says the death of women in domestic violence incidents is "harrowing". (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Ms Camm has remained staunch in her decision not to publicly state how many recommendations have been implemented, and how many are in progress or not implemented.

This is despite admitting that while in opposition, she was one of the loudest voices calling on the previous government for transparency about its progress.

"We are calmly, methodically working through those recommendations," she said.

She said a recommendation by the taskforce to create a domestic violence offender registry is "absolutely not off the table".

The minister also stated she wanted proposed breach bail, go to jail laws for youth offenders to be extended to include adults who commit domestic violence offences.

"High risk offenders, where there has been criminality or criminal offences charged, where they have breached bail, absolutely they should go to jail," she said.

This week, Premier David Crisafulli confirmed the government was actively considering expanding the proposed laws to include adults.

Opposition Leader Steven Miles said the government was hiding its progress in response to the report.

"The only reason to hide it is because you're ashamed of your lack of progress," he said.

'Futures being stolen'

DV Connect chief executive Joanne Jessop said every death was a tragedy.

"These are lives and futures being stolen … and it is really beholden on all of us to do more … to keep people safe across our communities," she said.

Ms Jessop said she believed there would be more deaths as a result of coercive control and violence in relationships than reported.

We can't predict domestic violence homicide Victims must always be believed. The uncomfortable truth, however, is that statistically, it is almost impossible to predict lethal family violence because it is so rare.

She said if "we are really serious about ending domestic violence deaths" more investment in prevention and early intervention was critical.

Ms Jessop said the key to prevention was working with people who use violence.

"Every time a person who uses violence takes responsibility for their behaviour and chooses a different path, we improve safety," she said.

"Every time that violence is interrupted, we actually make change or save a life."

World.title: Students walk out of school around the country to protest One Nation
World.content:
Students around the country have walked out of school to join protests in capital cities and some regions against One Nation and its leader Pauline Hanson.

The rallies have been condemned by Ms Hanson, who wrote a message to students on social media platform X (formerly Twitter), saying: "Whether you know it or not, One Nation and I are fighting for you."

In Melbourne, hundreds of students gathered outside the State Library in the CBD carrying anti-One Nation signs, banners and a pinata designed to look like Ms Hanson which was broken apart.

Organised by the National Union of Students, the rally saw speeches from both high school students and political leaders, including former Victorian Greens leader Samantha Ratnam.

Ms Ratnam said she was impressed by the turnout.

"It gives me hope that we can stop the rise of One Nation," she said.

"Everything is on the line right now."

Several students brought handmade signs to the protest in Melbourne. (ABC News)

The upcoming Victorian state election will be the first time year 12 student Corey Zalchendler will be able to vote, something they said they were very excited about.

"Since people under 18 can't vote I think they should come out and protest," Corey said.

"They should express their democratic rights and stand up for what they believe in, stand up for equality and rights."

Students joined the protest, voicing their opposition to racism, bigotry and capitalism. (ABC News: Sacha Payne)

The sentiment was shared by 15-year-old student Georgia Newton.

"I'm tired of the injustices that Pauline Hanson is threatening … and the whole One Nation party is threatening to do, if they go into office," she said.

"Do not run for office, and stop hating on the people who just want to be themselves."

She said her parents were supportive of her attending the protest.

"They think that the youth should be able to learn and do what they want," she said.

High school student Georgia says her parents supported her joining the protest. (ABC News)

One Nation supporters led away from rallies in Sydney, Brisbane

Protesters in Sydney carried homemade signs and a paper mache Pauline Hanson head in a protest against the One Nation leader and her policies.

A crowd of mostly students filled the square outside Sydney's Town Hall chanting against racism, sexism and homophobia.

Greens Newtown MP Jenny Leong spoke to cheers against racists, "including Pauline Hanson", asking the students to pledge to continue to attend rallies.

Chants included "high school, uni, teachers too, Pauline Hanson, we're coming for you" and "racist, sexist, anti-queer, Pauline Hanson not welcome here".

The crowd was told their attendance was a display of democracy. (ABC News: Emily Baker)

One year 9 student told the ABC he had received resistance from teachers before walking out of school, while others said they had received permission from their parents to skip school entirely.

"The media have gone crazy over the fact that high schoolers are walking out of school," one event organiser said to the crowd.

"This is what democracy looks like."

A woman chanting in support of One Nation was escorted away from the broader rally by police and event organisers.

In Brisbane, a One Nation supporter yelling "Pauline Hanson will save Australia" to a protest crowd of about 200 young people in King George Square was removed and arrested by police officers.

Police said the arrest was discontinued, and the man issued with a move-on direction.

About 200 people attended the Brisbane protest. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

Students for Palestine organiser and university student Connor Knight said he was pleased to see high school students in attendance.

"I think nothing is more important than people standing up against our society going backwards," he said.

"If students want to walk out of school, that's them making a statement that they think that is important."

Teenagers Emma Totzl and Mara Helmers attended today's protest in Brisbane. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

One Nation supporter Maree, who stumbled across the CBD protest, said it was concerning.

"There's so many young people here who have got this view that there's something wrong with democracy and capitalism," she said.

"There's a conflict there that they don't seem to understand."

Politicians tell students to stay in school

In response to the rallies around the country, Ms Hanson said schools "should teach young Australians how to think, not what to think".

"If you want to protest something, protest why your parents' wages are going backwards and the cost of everything is going up," the post said.

"The Labor Greens government is selling out your future, and you'll inherit a weaker, poorer and less safe country."

Earlier on Thursday, Victorian Premier Ben Carroll had a stern message for students thinking of attending the rally.

"You want to change the world, stay at school … focus on what your learning is in the classroom," he said.

"I understand they're angry with the sentiment and the policies of One Nation but the best way to change your future and the world is to get an education and to stay in school."

Victorian One Nation MP Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell also spoke out against the protest, urging students to stay in school.

"You have an amazing future ahead of you, don't waste it by listening to one group of people. Be critical, do your research and think about your future," she said.

World.title: Man died amid 'systemic failings' of 'overworked' health system, inquest finds
World.content:
A man, who died after his high-priority cardiac surgery was delayed, could have survived if the operation occurred sooner — but South Australia's overworked health system meant it "might have come at the cost of the chance of survival of another patient", a coroner has found.

Petar Josipovic, 62, died in the Royal Adelaide Hospital (RAH) on September 14, 2023, after he was placed on a waiting list for category one cardiac surgery in June that year — an operation which should have occurred within 30 days.

During the inquest last year, the court heard Mr Josipovic's surgery was scheduled 54 days later, on August 14, 2023, but was rescheduled multiple times.

He became unwell on August 24 and was rushed to hospital where he suffered a cardiac arrest.

He had successful emergency surgery early the next morning, but died from complications three weeks later.

State Coroner David Whittle today handed down his findings, and said that, on the balance of probabilities, Mr Josipovic's death "would have been unlikely if surgery was performed" on or before August 22, 2023.

However, he said the "opportunity to perform it earlier did not genuinely arise".

Mr Whittle said he was impressed with the witnesses who gave evidence and did "not make any finding that decisions that led to the cancellations were the result of ill-will or lack of due care".

He noted, however, that there was "a wider cohort of concerning patients" at the time.

"This was a case where systemic failings of an overworked system resulted in the inability to detect the extent of Mr Josipovic's deterioration before it was too late," Mr Whittle said.

The coroner made two recommendations to SA's health minister. (ABC News: Dean Faulkner)

He said had Mr Josipovic's surgery gone ahead as scheduled on August 14, 2023, his "chance of survival was high".

"Of course, I observe that proceeding with the surgery on that day might have come at the cost of the chance of survival of another patient and that difficult decisions were made," he said.

"I am in the end unable to conclude that there was a genuine opportunity to make a different decision."

Delay 'exponentially increased risk'

During the inquest, the court heard Mr Josipovic's son, Nick Josipovic, had written to the coroner on the day his father died, raising concerns about delays to his surgery.

He had told the inquest he had pleaded for his father's surgery to occur in the scheduled date, because his family "had great concerns" he would not survive.

In his findings, Mr Whittle said Mr Josipovic did not go to the emergency department on earlier occasions when he was invited to, which would "reasonably give clinicians a sense of ease about the seriousness of his deterioration and also prevented the physical examination of his condition that was necessary to fully appreciate his risk".

He said the inquest had been told that Mr Josipovic's surgery would have cost less than $75,000 if it occurred electively, but the ultimate cost of his care following his emergency surgery admission was $250,000.

"The delay in the performance of Mr Josipovic's cardiac surgery exponentially increased the risk to his life and the financial cost to the state," Mr Whittle said.

Petar Josipovic's son Nick outside the inquest in 2025. (ABC News)

Mr Whittle noted there had been several improvements to the manner of delivery of cardiothoracic services at the RAH since Mr Josipovic's death, and noted he had heard evidence there was now "better oversight of waiting lists" at the hospital.

But, he said even with other improvements that had been made, including increased operating capacity, "more can be done".

He made two recommendations to Health Minister Blair Boyer, including that an external review be conducted to consider matters including the referral process, clinic capacity, the costs and benefits of an additional theatre list and surgical cancellations.

Mr Whittle also recommended clear guidelines be developed about the information and advice to be given to patients awaiting cardiothoracic surgery who report clinical deterioration.

Mr Whittle also expressed his sincere condolences to Mr Josipovic's family, noting his son Nick had given evidence and attended the hearing each day.

World.title: Investigators 'misled' alleged victim of police assaults, court told
World.content:
Two police officers charged with assaulting and unlawfully restraining a prisoner in a regional Queensland watch house have asked a court to put an end to criminal proceedings against them.

The District Court in Cairns has heard Charlton Bong, 25, was tasered, cuffed and left alone in a padded cell for about two and a half hours at the Mareeba watch house in Far North Queensland on January 20, 2024.

Senior Constables Andrew David Couchman, 54, and Ulrich Weiss, 45, were investigated by the police Ethical Standards Command over the incident and charged with criminal offences, including assault and deprivation of liberty.

A trial has been listed for next month, however, defence barrister David Jones KC, for Senior Constable Couchman, today argued for a permanent stay of the case.

He acknowledged it would be an "extraordinary measure", but said there was otherwise a risk of the "trial starting under the shadow of police misconduct".

Investigator 'misled' alleged victim

The officers' application for a permanent stay of the charges followed a January 2026 committal hearing in which investigating officer Detective Senior Sergeant Kim Cavill conceded she added a line into Mr Bong's sworn statement saying he did not consent to the force used against him.

The court has previously heard Mr Bong could not read or write and had been experiencing mental health issues at the watch house.

Mr Jones told the court on Tuesday that Detective Senior Sergeant Cavill "misled" Mr Bong.

"Even after reading the final paragraph to Mr Bong, Detective Senior Sergeant Cavill said, 'That's from my recordings of what you have told me previously,'" Mr Jones told the court.

"That is a lie. That is deception, and that is deception from an officer of the Ethical Standards Command."

Andrew David Couchman (right) leaves court with his lawyers, including barrister David Jones KC (far left). (ABC Far North: Conor Byrne)

The court heard there would be two issues at trial: consent and justification.

Mr Bong gave evidence at an earlier pre-trial hearing, telling the court he deserved to be tasered because he was hearing voices and acting violently.

"Whilst the word consent wasn't used, it is more closely aligned with an answer that would assist the applicants in this case rather than the Crown," Mr Jones said.

Mr Jones said it had been left to the defence to "try and unravel what is unreliable" ahead of next month's trial, including "what [Mr Bong] might have been led to believe over time".

Charlton Bong was tasered and cuffed while at the Mareeba watch house in January 2024. (Supplied: QPS)

Senior Constable Weiss's lawyer Calvin Gnech said the "contamination" of the case began well before the extra line in Mr Bong's statement was typed.

Mr Gnech said Mr Bong's "understanding of the incident has been shaped by the investigating conduct", including multiple formal interviews and a pre-trial hearing.

"Mr Bong's capacity to reset, give independent evidence at trial — genuinely independent of any of the contaminating influences — is at best speculative, and at worst, impossible," Mr Gnech told the court.

" That is a prejudice that any accused should not be faced with or have to even overcome when entitled to a fair trial. "

Calvin Gnech says the case against his client was "contaminated" during the investigation. (ABC Far North: Conor Byrne)

Mr Jones said the Ethical Standards Command investigation was neither impartial nor objective, and amounted to "improper conduct".

"If any unit of the Queensland Police Service should know better, it is that unit," he told the court.

Ruling due next week

Crown prosecutor Christian Peters told the court it was a "false characterisation" to suggest the investigation was prejudiced.

Mr Peters said Mr Bong was a "vulnerable Indigenous man in custody at the watch house" and that the sequence of events was entirely captured on video.

"[Mr Bong] is a person who will come along and be able to give evidence about his recollection of the incidents themselves," he said.

Mr Peters said the "state of all of the evidence in this matter" did not give rise to a level of unfairness that would warrant a permanent stay of the charges.

Charlton Bong outside court after giving evidence at an earlier hearing in May. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

"Whether or not [Mr Bong] consented, whether or not it was justified, whether or not the investigating officer impugned that particular concept, are all things the applicants, in my submission, are not prevented from pursuing at their trial," Mr Peters argued.

The court heard the Crown would rely on expert witnesses in its case against Senior Constables Couchman and Weiss, and that a jury could still conclude Mr Bong did not consent to the force used against him.

"There are other witnesses that point to the fact it was not necessary or justified," he said.

Senior Constable Couchman was present for today's hearing while Senior Constable Weiss's appearance was excused.

Judge Dean Morzone KC has reserved his decision and is due to rule on the application next week.

World.title: A second plane of greyhounds lands in Qld after New Zealand racing ban
World.content:
Up to ten per cent of New Zealand's greyhound racing industry has relocated from that country to Queensland, after the sport was banned in the country.

One flight, containing about 70 dogs landed at Toowoomba Wellcamp Airport today, while another containing a similar number arrived last week.

New Zealand announced it 2024 it would ban greyhound racing from August 1 this year, due to animal welfare concerns.

The country was home to about 1,500 racing dogs before the ban. 140 dogs equates to almost 10 per cent of their racing population.

Images taken by an activist group show greyhounds being loaded onto a plane in New Zealand. (Supplied: Grassroots Campaigns Aotearoa)

Dr Alison Vaughan, the senior scientific officer from the Royal New Zealand Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, told ABC Radio Brisbane the dogs were being sent for racing, not rehoming.

"This goes against the intent of the ban in New Zealand although it is still technically legal unfortunately," she said.

"We're hugely disappointed. Greyhound racing in whatever country it's being practised in carries a significant and inherent risk of serious injury and death."

Dr Vaughan said she was concerned the dogs would end up racing at The Q, a new venue in Ipswich which has recorded a number of injuries and deaths since it opened in 2025.

"Queensland has a higher rate than we saw in New Zealand. And in New Zealand we banned it due to injuries," she said.

A greyhound being led into a crate. (Supplied: Grassroots Campaigns Aotearoa)

"Organising a charter flight, just a single charter flight, costs in the hundreds of thousands [of dollars].

"And this would have been money that would have otherwise been transferred to rehomed greyhounds as pets in New Zealand."

The ABC revealed plans for the flights in June, when Queensland Racing Integrity Commission also said it had "received enquiries in relation to the relocation of New Zealand trainers".

QRIC is yet to respond to the ABC's requests for comment for this story.

The dogs are also expected to be raced in New South Wales, with one local club there — Century Park Racing — taking to social media to say some of the dogs will join its training ranks.

The club said in the post it was willing to assist others to make the trip from New Zealand to Australia.

It's believed to be the second plane of greyhounds to touch down in Australia from New Zealand in the last week. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

Queensland supportive of industry

Queensland's Racing Minister Tim Mander said he was not aware of Thursday's flight and the government had not assisted in the relocation.

But he said the dogs and trainers were "looking to compete somewhere" and the State Government supported greyhound racing.

"It's a big industry and it makes a significant economic contribution to our state. It employs thousands of people both directly and indirectly," he said.

"We've made significant investment in facilities and intend to maintain our commitment to it."

Mr Mander said the government had "many, many regulations and guidelines" around dog safety and they treated animal welfare "very importantly".

Queensland's Racing Minister Tim Mander said he was not aware of the flight. (ABC News)

"People are bringing dogs over I imagine with their trainers," he said.

"Their responsibility is to house them and look after them.

"So, they would all be under the conditions that apply to dogs that are in the industry. They need to meet those conditions."

New Zealand's Greyhound Transition Agency, a time-limited organisation set up to ensure racing greyhounds are cared for and rehomed, said it only cared for dogs whose owners transferred ownership to them.

"We have been made aware of the flights, but we have not taken part in facilitating any proposal by owners to export their greyhounds for racing," a spokesperson said.

"While racing has finished in New Zealand, owners still have time to decide whether to transfer ownership of their commercial racing industry dogs to the Transition Agency.

"This allows owners time to consider their options, given this may be a significant change."

The Queensland Racing Integrity Commission did not respond to the ABC's request for comment. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

The spokesperson said the country's racing agency, Greyhound Racing New Zealand, had committed to providing a list of dogs travelling to Australia on the charter flights to them.

"We will cross-check this list against our ownership records and share relevant information with … Australian greyhound racing authorities," they said.

"Any greyhound transferred to the Transition Agency will be deregistered from racing and therefore cannot race outside of New Zealand."

'Significant pressure' to rehome retired dogs

The RSPCA in Queensland said it was also concerned about the decision to send greyhounds to the state.

"When New Zealand announced it would end greyhound racing, many hoped it would mark the beginning of a safer future for the dogs involved," a spokesperson said.

The RSPCA said it is already trouble rehoming retired greyhounds. (ABC News: Robert Koenig-Luck)

"Queensland already faces significant pressure to find suitable homes for retired greyhounds.

"Adding more dogs to that system risks increasing the rehoming burden at a time when the focus should be on securing safe, suitable futures for the greyhounds already needing homes."

The federal Department of Agriculture has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Solomon rubbishes rumours of rifts with Essendon coaching candidates
World.content:
Interim Essendon coach Dean Solomon has described a rumoured falling-out with Mark McVeigh as like an "episode of Home and Away".

After Solomon chose not to put his hand up to be the Bombers' full-time coach, Essendon are closing in on announcing a leader as soon as next week.

McVeigh has been tipped to win the job, even ahead of Essendon icon James Hird.

It has led to suggestions of a rift among the trio, something Solomon has strenuously denied.

Solomon (centre) says there is no ill-feeling towards either Hird (left) or McVeigh (right) after pulling out of the Essendon coaching race. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"We don't know where they've come from — they're rumours," Solomon said.

"[McVeigh's has been] one of my best mates since the age of 15.

"I've known Hirdy since the age of 17.

"The talks with me potentially not being here next year, whether that stimulated a bit of that conversation, we're unsure.

"But I feel like it's a bit of an episode of [long-running Australian TV soapie] Home and Away.

McVeigh, currently an assistant with Sydney, has been touted as the favourte to win the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

"There's nothing there. We all want to see this club heading in the right direction."

Solomon, McVeigh and Hird all played together at the Bombers, with Solomon and Hird playing in Essendon's most recent premiership side in 2000. McVeigh played with the pair in a losing grand final in 2001.

The trio also worked together briefly at GWS when McVeigh was the Giants' interim coach in 2022.

Solomon initially declared he would stay on at the Bombers next year, even if he wasn't senior coach.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But his family remains living in northern NSW, complicating matters for him.

"Part of the process of thinking about going in the process for the senior coaching role was sitting down with my family and talking about that," Solomon said.

"My wife and kids live in northern NSW.

"I've had 10 to 11 months away from them at the moment.

"Is that sustainable long-term? It's probably not."

Solomon stressed the next coach didn't need to be an Essendon person, referencing the legendary Kevin Sheedy, who grew up supporting the Bombers but whose playing career was at Richmond.

"He just needs to be the right person," Solomon said.

"A lot of people surrounding our football club are really frustrated.

"We want to be great, and we want to be great really quickly.

"This is a big job and it's an exciting challenge."

AAP

World.title: Australia v Bangladesh LIVE: Smith falls short amid Darwin batting collapse, CA boss addresses Gardner-Voll affair
World.content:
Todd Greenberg addressed the Ash Gardner-Georgia Voll relationship on SEN during the lunch break and said additional policies have been put in place by Cricket Australia to ensure there are no conflicts of interest at selection given Gardner remains Australian vice-captain.

“It is a very personal matter for the player, and I think there’s a level of respect that needs to go with that,” the Cricket Australia CEO said. “Cricket’s got very strong respect-at-work policies, so we’ve got a policy that’s been developed over time that can deal with these sorts of things.

Australia’s Ash Gardner. Getty Images

“Ash is a highly regarded leader in our system. The CA board make leadership decisions and have oversight over all leadership decisions. Ash is our vice-captain for a reason, because she’s highly regarded, but what we will do is in situations where there are personal relationships, is make sure there are additional guardrails, so the perception of conflict or conflict itself, talking about things like selection, are handled appropriately and respectfully.

“We’ve got policies in place but we will put additional ones in place given Ash is now vice-captain. If there are relationships that have been disclosed and they have been, then we will make sure that conflict – perceived or real – around selections are removed, so Ash is not involved in those things.

“It was new news in the media, but for those that were in the team and leading the team, we’ve been well across this for a period of time.”

Greenberg reiterated that the episode did not influence the decision to appoint Sophie Molineux captain, ahead of Gardner, earlier this year.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Mother of complainant ‘J’ gives evidence after legal issue triggers adjournment
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day seven of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Court reporter Clare Sibthorpe and I will be bringing you the latest from the hearing today.

If day seven looks familiar, you’re right. Yesterday was to be the seventh day of the trial, but the Crown foreshadowed that it wanted to amend seven of the charges in the case. This triggered an adjournment for the parties to make legal arguments.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Thursday. Oscar Colman

After hearing those arguments, Judge Glenn Walsh said the Crown did not require the court’s permission to make the changes, which do not relate to the alleged physical acts in the case. He concluded that it did not result in prejudice to Jones and his right to a fair trial.

Jones’ lawyers did not object to an amendment to one of the charges but had opposed the amendments to the remaining six.

The trial is expected to resume in earnest today in the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre building with more evidence relating to complainant “J”, the first witness to give evidence in the trial.

In the first week of the trial, the court heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted “J”, a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12. Jones denies the claims.

On Tuesday, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what they say he told them about the alleged assaults.

His brother said he had not witnessed Jones acting inappropriately towards “J”, but that the complainant told him in 2024, after Jones’ arrest, that he was one the men who had come forward.

The ex-girlfriend of “J” said he confided in her 20 years ago that Jones had touched him inappropriately. She said he looked like he had “seen a ghost” before he made the disclosure and swore her to secrecy.

Her evidence continues today. The mother of “J” and his former sporting coach are also slated to give evidence.

While we don’t expect to hear from him today, a man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence. He may start his evidence as early as Friday.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and his barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: ‘We’ve been very clear in private’ what US needs from AUKUS: Pentagon
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAUKUS ‘We’ve been very clear in private’ what US needs from AUKUS: Pentagon Michael Koziol August 13, 2026 — 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The Pentagon’s policy chief says the US has been “very clear in private” with the Albanese government about what is expected from Australia under the AUKUS agreement, while underlining the strategic importance of HMAS Stirling to the US. Elbridge Colby, who was one of the prominent AUKUS sceptics in the Trump administration before the US president’s declaration that the deal was “full steam ahead”, said the Pentagon was very pleased with the progress on AUKUS since its review was handed down last year. Undersecretary of War for Policy at the US Pentagon Elbridge Colby. Bloomberg Asked about future US activity at Submarine Rotational Force-West – the stationing of US nuclear-powered submarines, and later Australia’s, at HMAS Stirling near Perth – Colby said the facility was “tremendously important, and is one of the key values that benefit not just the United States but Australia itself”. SRF-West was recently the subject of a political row after Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy told the ABC from Washington that US submarines would only be there for five years until 2032, before correcting himself and acknowledging the US presence would be “ongoing”.



At stake was the question of whether nuclear-armed submarines would be allowed to rotate through HMAS Stirling given Australia’s obligation to maintain a nuclear-weapon-free zone under the Treaty of Rarotonga. Related Article AUKUS ‘Bridge’ Colby: Who is the ‘maverick’ putting AUKUS through the wringer? Colby, who is Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s undersecretary for policy, did not directly answer when asked about nuclear-armed submarines at SRF-West after 2032. But he said the Pentagon and broader Trump administration have a “very tight discussion and a very clear understanding” about AUKUS with the Australian government, without detailing those discussions. “They know what is required, we’ve been very clear in private with them,” he said on a briefing call with reporters. “[That is] designed to give everybody a reasonable, stable and realistic set of expectations to achieve this historic ambition that will put us all in a stronger place.



“We see a deep alignment of thinking … Australia really sees things through the lens of collective defence and a strategy of deterrence by denial designed to sustain a balance of power in this key region.” Colby also did not directly answer when asked about the current production rate of Virginia-class nuclear submarines, which the Pentagon recently admitted was languishing at about 1.1 to 1.2 boats a year, when it needed to be 2.33 to meet AUKUS requirements. Loading “We remain optimistic but also clear-eyed about what we all need to do,” he said. “We will just keep knocking down the targets on our side. We have every expectation the Australian side will do the same.” Colby added that the Pentagon was seeing “more and more” energy and focus from Canberra, and there was “no better ally” than Australia.



Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Richard Marles’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Related Article AUKUS ‘It won’t be a US military base’: Cook stands firm on HMAS Stirling future The remarks come amid an ongoing public inquiry into the $368 billion-plus defence pact headed by AUKUS sceptics including former Labor minister and rock star Peter Garrett. Former Liberal prime minister Malcolm Turnbull, whose submarine deal with France was cancelled by his successor Scott Morrison, recently told the inquiry it was unlikely the US would double its rate of production in time, and there was a real risk Australia received no Virginia-class boats. “This risk is acknowledged everywhere but in Canberra,” he said.

Three students from Sydney’s prestigious Scots College have been charged with sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl in an eastern suburbs alley way.

A 13-year-old boy and two 14-year-old boys were arrested on Thursday over the alleged July 22 attack.

Three Scots College students have been charged with sexually assaulting a teenage girl. Louise Kennerley

World.title: It’s the most dangerous tackle in the NRL. Dolphins coach says this player is being targeted
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 It’s the most dangerous tackle in the NRL. Dolphins coach says this player is being targeted Christian Nicolussi August 13, 2026 — 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf has called on the NRL to protect Herbie Farnworth after a string of hip-drop style tackles on his star centre in recent weeks raised fears it is only a matter of time before he suffers a series injury. Farnworth has been hit low and from behind on at least five occasions, prompting Woolf to ask referees to monitor the situation as a matter of urgency. Brisbane’s Kotoni Staggs became the latest player penalised for a hip-drop tackle on Farnworth, in the 47th minute of last Saturday’s 40-32 come-from-behind Dolphins win. In round 18, Newcastle players collected Farnworth twice within six minutes, with neither tackle sanctioned.



There was a dubious tackle from behind approaching the hour mark in a game against the Wests Tigers in round 16, while Farnworth was convinced Warriors winger Dallin Watene-Zelezniak had executed a hip-drop tackle during a game in round eight, only for the referee to order him to play the ball. No player has yet been charged for a hip-drop tackle on Farnworth because the match review committee will only punish a player if the bulk of their bodyweight lands on the attacking player’s legs. But the Englishman has had to receive treatment on more than one occasion. After this masthead pointed out the string of dangerous tackles on Farnworth from this season alone, Woolf said he was concerned that if officials did not penalise some of the defensive efforts on Farnworth, fans would potentially be robbed of watching a genuine superstar through the finals series. “Because Herbie is so big and powerful and he can break the line, it often leaves players swinging off the back of him and trying to bring him to ground,” Woolf told this masthead.



“It’s a concern because it’s a dangerous tackle that happens on a regular basis. All the players are aware of the hip-drop tackle. We look for it more, and we talk about them more. “Herbie is one of the elite players in our competition, and it’s only a matter of time before one of those tackles ends badly and he suffers a serious injury.” Woolf said Cronulla’s Jesse Ramien was beaten by Farnworth during the Sharks’ 66-0 win after Origin III, but had placed his knee on the ground and tried to drag his opposite centre to the ground with an excellent technique. The far more common sight, Woolf said, was a player more often than not the third man into the tackle launching himself into Farnworth’s legs.



The 26-year-old Farnworth has enjoyed another brilliant season at Redcliffe, with growing speculation he will head to the open market on November 1 then join the Sydney Roosters for the 2028 season. Woolf was aware of the external interest in Farnworth but remained optimistic the Dolphins could strike a deal to retain him before the World Cup in October. “We’re comfortable with the situation, we’re confident that Herbie wants to be at our club, and we want him at the club long-term – it’s a conversation we’ll have as soon as our season is finished,” Woolf said. Related Article NRL 2026 Why South Sydney should thank Sam Burgess for their $4200-a-week bargain buy



The Dolphins have one of the best attacking backlines in the NRL, including Farnworth, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Selwyn Cobbo and Jack Bostock – all current Origin representatives – as well as Jamayne Isaako, Kodi Nikorima and Isaiya Katoa. The Dolphins will look to keep their top-four hopes alive when they travel to the Northern Beaches to play Manly on Friday evening. After the Sea Eagles, they play Parramatta, the Roosters and Titans before embarking on the club’s first finals campaign. World.title: Taste testing the Japanese melon at the heart of a political stink
World.content:
WorldAsiaForeign relations Taste testing the Japanese melon at the heart of a political stink Zach Hope August 13, 2026 — 3:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It is the fruit that has Canberra talking and put the prime minister in the hot seat. The Japanese Shizuoka crown melon. Loading Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi gifted a couple of the high-status fruits to her counterpart, Anthony Albanese, during a recent visit to Australia. The embassy made clear the melons were purchased in Australia from one of the businesses that have been allowed to import them since March. So nothing to see here, right?



Not quite. In a now-infamous podcast at The Lodge on July 3 with ribald host Nikki Osborne, Albanese brought up the melons in response to a question about the most “crap gift” he ever got. Of course, Albanese didn’t say Takaichi’s gift was crap. Rather, he said it “was pretty strange but ended up being quite good”. Fair enough. World.title: The secret supply route Russia is using to sustain the Iran war
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeMiddle East at war The secret supply route Russia is using to sustain the Iran war Glen E Howard August 13, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Russia has quietly established a new strategic supply route to Iran across the Caspian Sea. Called by some the Caspian Express, this logistics corridor has become the backbone of Vladimir Putin’s effort to arm Tehran while allowing both countries to circumvent US maritime pressure in the Persian Gulf. Moscow applied this model during the Syrian civil war when it sustained the regime of Bashar al-Assad through a maritime supply route sometimes termed the Syrian Express. Operating for nearly a decade between occupied Crimea and the Syrian port of Tartus, the supply corridor allowed Moscow to reinforce its expeditionary forces despite Western sanctions and diplomatic pressure. Turkey closed the Bosphorus to warships following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, squeezing the route, before the lifeline was cut by the end of the Syrian regime in 2024. Since Vladimir Putin extended Russia’s aggression against Ukraine in 2022, Iran has become a vital Russian ally. Kristina Solovyova/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP Today, Russia has replicated that approach in the Caspian, transforming the inland sea into its logistical backbone for its military partnership with Iran. The strategic consequences are becoming increasingly visible as “Gulf War III” expands to the region. Earlier this year, Israel carried out air strikes against Iran’s Caspian naval base at Bandar Anzali, destroying port facilities and several boats in the first-ever use of Israeli air power in the Caspian region. At the end of July, Ukraine carried out a drone strike on an Iranian commercial vessel killing one sailor in the Caspian, which prompted Tehran to consider retaliatory strikes against the Ukrainian port of Odesa.



Since Putin extended Russia’s aggression against Ukraine in 2022, Iran has become a vital Russian ally – supplying Moscow with $US2.7 billion ($3.8 billion) in ballistic and air-defence missiles, including hundreds of Fath-360 short-range ballistic missiles and 200 surface-to-air missiles, while Russia has spent more than $US4 billion on Iranian military equipment since late 2021. Iran provided the key components and technology for Putin’s fleet of Shahed drones and helped Moscow establish production facilities at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone to manufacture up to 6000 units a year. As many as four Iranian Caspian ports are working around the clock to import wheat, feed and oil as Tehran reroutes essential trade through the inland sea due to the American blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Loading Meanwhile, in the northern Caspian, the Russian port of Olya has become Moscow’s primary transit hub for importing Iranian drone components and ammunition. Consequently, both Russia and Iran rely on the landlocked Caspian as an indispensable supply line for their respective war efforts. In a striking historical irony, this same “Persian Corridor” across the Caspian once served as a vital lifeline during World War II, when massive quantities of American Lend-Lease assistance flowed through Persia to sustain the Soviet war effort against Nazi Germany.



Today, Moscow is once again relying on this historic corridor, confident that the Caspian remains an untouchable sanctuary. For decades, Russia has treated the Caspian Sea as a protected “bastion” beyond Western reach, where its naval forces launched Kalibr cruise missiles against Syria in 2015, and more recently against Ukraine from its missile range at Kapustin Yar using Putin’s new Wunderwaffe weapon – the Oreshnik ballistic missile. Because the Caspian is landlocked, the United States can do nothing as a maritime power to prevent Russia from shipping Iran supplies that would otherwise pass through the Strait of Hormuz, now blockaded by the US Navy. This geographic reality plays directly into Moscow’s broader geopolitical ambitions as the Caspian becomes the centrepiece of a North-South transport corridor linking Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran and ultimately India while bypassing maritime choke points controlled by the West. In doing so, Moscow and Tehran are operationalising Sir Halford Mackinder’s Heartland theory by creating a landlocked Eurasian logistics network that blunts Western sea power. Interdicting these supply lines has therefore taken on greater urgency as Moscow has actively rebuilt Iran’s offensive capabilities during recent pauses in fighting with the US in the Gulf. American officials told The New York Times that Russia helped Iran restock after it lost 60 per cent of its drone arsenal during the war.



As the regional dimension of the Iran-US conflict expands, the Trump administration must decide whether to contest the Caspian Express before it becomes the permanent logistical spine of the Russia-Iran partnership. Related Article Middle East at war Iran’s drones gave Russia a deadly boost in Ukraine. Now they are blitzing the Gulf The White House has already laid the diplomatic foundation by supporting an Armenia-Azerbaijan peace agreement and by launching the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity. It should now build on that success by developing a regional strategy that leverages Azerbaijan’s emergence as a rising middle power in the South Caucasus while enabling Ukraine to sustain military pressure on the Caspian Express without risk of direct US involvement. History shows that wars are often decided not only on the battlefield but along the supply routes that sustain them. The Syrian Express prolonged one war for years. The Caspian Express now underpins the Russia-Iran strategic partnership and Tehran’s effort to outlast the United States in a war that is now going into its sixth month. Whether the Caspian Express remains Moscow’s strategic lifeline to Iran – or ultimately fails – will depend on whether Washington adopts a regional strategy capable of contesting the emergence of a new Persian Corridor and stymying Russian efforts to arm Iran.



Glen E. Howard is president of The Saratoga Foundation, a US non-profit organisation researching Russia, China, Iran and North Korea and the countries’ interests in the rest of the world.
